newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Jeers and cheers for Mandela's global peace drive.
newsitem.headline: Jeers and cheers for Mandela's global peace drive.

text.p: South African President Nelson Mandela, already helping the search for peace in at least 10 countries, plans to renew his efforts to end the conflicts in Sudan and East Timor later this month.
Not everyone is convinced, however, that either Mandela or South Africa have much to offer to world peace.
Officials said Mandela was likely to meet Sudanese rebel leader John Garang and U.N. special representative for East Timor Jamseed Marker before the end of August.
"President Mandela has emerged as a leader with stature far beyond our borders," said deputy foreign minister Aziz Pahad.

"We're also the newest boys on the block and sometimes it is felt by belligerent groups that South Africa has no hidden agenda. Increasingly, we are getting involved in trying to resolve conflicts," he told Reuters.

Mandela, 79, has not scored one unqualified success since 1994, when he led his own country from the conflict of apartheid through an almost miraculously peaceful transition to a democracy largely accepted by blacks and whites.

Some recent mediation efforts have led to blunders such as the delivery of a personal letter to Indonesian President Suharto about East Timor to the embassy of Portugal, the territory's former colonial power, which leaked it to the media.

Mandela's credibility was further dented by his erroneous announcement after talking to Kofi Annan on a cellular telephone that the U.N. secretary-general would make a surprise visit to South Africa to discuss the East Timor initiative.

"A number of interventions by the President himself in African crises...have raised considerable doubts about Pretoria's ability to influence these events," political analyst Greg Mills wrote in the Sunday Independent.

"The President's attempts to bring democracy to Nigeria and reconciliation to Angola...and to nudge King Mswati III of Swaziland to introduce democratic reforms speedily must all be counted more as failures than successes," he said.

Denis Venter of the Pretoria-based Africa Institute told a conference in Addis Ababa recently South Africa was slipping dangerously from the principles that underpinned the country's own transition towards political pragmatism.
"South Africa should be uncompromising in its determination to speak out against genocide and other atrocities on the African continent," he said.
"It should be clear that South Africa does not accept...that the spirit of pan-Africanism requires it to keep silent about, for example, the phony democracies of Kenya and Zimbabwe."
Venter's paper drew a written protest and a charge of racism from the Organisation of African Unity.
In another bitter rebuke, Nigerian Information Minister Walter Ofonagoro told the Nigerian Guild of Editors recently: "South Africa is a white country with a black head of state."
Tony Leon, leader of the small Democratic Party, said many people had feared a shift towards Marxism when Mandela was elected the country's first black president in 1994.
"Instead, we're getting the Marx Brothers. This is Loony Toons," he said.
Pahad, who generally is charged with the detail of Mandela's often ambitious efforts to spread the gospel of reconciliation, insists South Africa does have an important role to play.
"We are learning as we run. But, with the support of other countries, South Africa is beginning to play a new role in key issues that are unfolding.
"South Africa, while it is true that we are still learning, has been able to play a particular role in broader issues than we had expected to be involved in," he said.

So far, Mandela has intervened to some extent in conflicts in or involving Lesotho, Swaziland, Angola, Mozambique, Sudan, Algeria, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Libya, East Timor, Thailand, Northern Ireland and even the Middle East.
Pahad said the incidents of the letter and the misheard conversation with Annan were mistakes unlikely to be repeated.
"Generally, as a country and after many years of isolation, we have entered an international arena that is transforming quite radically.
"I'm not saying we have a magic wand. We just happened to come in at the right time, when the whole of the international environment was changing," he said.
